title: Asylum Win Caps Immigrant's Two-Year Detention as Courts Weigh Third-Country Deportations
excerpt: Celestin Dima fled torture in Burkina Faso, won protection from deportation — and was then held for two years while ICE shopped for a third country to take him. His asylum grant comes as the Supreme Court lets the practice resume.
body:
• Celestin Dima, a gay asylum-seeker from Burkina Faso who was kidnapped and tortured by police after being outed, has won asylum in the United States — capping more than two years in ICE detention.
  • Dima was granted protection from deportation to Burkina Faso in August 2025, but ICE kept him locked up while shopping for a third country willing to take him — first Ghana, where homosexuality is punishable by up to three years in jail, then Cameroon and Uganda.
  • "If you send me back to the countries you mentioned, it's better to send me to my own country. Even if they kill me there, it's better than sending me to countries where they burn homosexuals," Dima told an ICE official.
  • What it means for immigrants: the win lands as the Supreme Court lets the administration resume rapid third-country deportations (6-3 ruling, September 29) while agreeing to hear full arguments in December — and as it takes up the mandatory-detention policy that kept Dima caged after he won his case.

Celestin Dima spent more than two years in immigration detention and came within hours of being deported to the Republic of Congo, a country where he had never lived — shackled on a deportation flight before the grant intervened. On September 23, an immigration judge in New York City granted him asylum — uncontested by the Department of Homeland Security — a victory that closes one man's ordeal while the courts wrestle with the policies that created it.

Why he fled

Dima fled Burkina Faso, the landlocked West African nation, after being outed as gay, kidnapped, and later targeted by the military and tortured by police. He crossed the US-Mexico border in late July 2024 seeking refuge and was detained. A Biden-era rule barred him from asylum because he crossed between official ports of entry — so in August 2025, a judge at Arizona's Eloy Immigration Court granted him withholding of removal from Burkina Faso, ruling that sending him home would likely bring further persecution.

Under any previous administration, lawyers say, that decision would have meant release. Instead, Dima stayed locked inside an ICE detention center for nearly another year while the government searched for a third country willing to accept him. He was one of at least 120 immigrants ICE kept detained in Arizona after judges barred deportation to their home countries, according to an Arizona Center for Investigative Reporting analysis — and more than half were held beyond the six-month mark at which the Supreme Court has said the government risks violating constitutional limits.

The third-country search

Officials first sought to deport Dima to Ghana, where homosexuality is punishable by up to three years in jail. A judge ruled he could not safely be sent there either. ICE then raised Cameroon and Uganda — the latter home to one of the world's harshest anti-LGBT laws. The possibilities terrified him.

"If you send me back to the countries you mentioned, it's better to send me to my own country," he recalled telling an ICE official at a hearing. "Even if they kill me there, it's better than sending me to countries where they burn homosexuals." He also feared chain refoulement — that a third country would simply send him back to Burkina Faso, bypassing the American judge's protections.

While detained at Eloy, Dima grew so sick with worry that he stopped eating for stretches; after repeatedly refusing food, he said, he was placed in solitary confinement for two weeks. "I've lost hope," he told AZCIR from his cell in June. "Right now, I don't even know what I want. To this day, I regret coming to the United States."

"Unconstitutional removal cannot cure unconstitutional detention."

— U.S. District Judge Diane J. Humetewa, ordering the release of Dima and other detainees

The release — and the re-arrest

In March, the Florence Immigrant and Refugee Rights Project filed a joint habeas petition for Dima and eight others — including an Iranian woman arrested after filming a video about the Kurdish minority and a Chilean man tortured as an Indigenous Mapuche — arguing their indefinite detention was unlawful. On June 29, a federal judge granted the petition and ordered release within 48 hours. The next morning, a bus pulled into a Phoenix church parking lot; twelve people got out, all just freed from ICE detention. Dima sat stunned at a table, eating grapes, cherries and Costco roast chicken prepared by volunteers. "I cannot express myself — the way I'm feeling," he said, chuckling.

In ordering the release, U.S. District Judge Diane J. Humetewa rejected the government's reliance on potential third-country deportation to justify continued detention: "Unconstitutional removal cannot cure unconstitutional detention."

Freedom lasted less than three weeks. Dima moved to the Bronx, planning to apply for a work permit — but at a mandatory ICE check-in on July 17 in Lower Manhattan, agents took him back into custody, telling him they planned to deport him but refusing to say where.

The bigger fight

Dima's case sits at the centre of the administration's third-country deportation strategy. Historically, the U.S. removed people with withholding protections to third countries only in extraordinary circumstances — in 2017, just 21 such removals occurred. The second Trump administration changed that, directing DHS to review cases of people granted withholding or Convention Against Torture protections and negotiating more than $32 million in agreements to persuade foreign governments — including roughly half a dozen African nations, most recently Burundi — to accept deportees with no ties to their countries.

On September 29, the Supreme Court ruled 6-3 that the administration can resume rapidly deporting migrants to countries other than their own while litigation continues, lifting a lower court's block. Full oral arguments are set for December. Separately, on October 1, the Court agreed to review the mandatory-detention policy that kept Dima locked up after winning his case — a policy nine federal appeals courts have ruled unlawful.

Detaining an immigrant costs taxpayers about $150 per person per day, according to DHS. As of June, more than 8,000 of the roughly 66,000 people in immigration detention nationwide had been held at least six months — more than double the number in September 2024.

What's next

Dima's asylum grant gives him what withholding never could: a path to permanent status and, eventually, citizenship — and protection from the third-country machinery that nearly swallowed him. But the December Supreme Court arguments will decide whether thousands of others in his position face the same limbo. "We're up against a bit of a tidal wave," said Katharine Ruhl, the Florence Project attorney who represented Dima. "We have many more clients who we have not been able to represent because of our limited capacity, who are in the same circumstance."

nri_angle: The case is a window into the detention-and-deportation machinery that also ensnares South Asian asylum-seekers; the Supreme Court's December arguments on third-country removals and mandatory detention will shape the landscape for every immigrant community.
author: Diaspora Desk
